To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the crystal structure of the γ subunit (γS) of archaeal eIF2 in complex with GDP and a nonhydrolyzably bound GTP analog (GDPCP) reveals the active state of the γS subunit and provides insight into the molecular mechanism underlying the conformational transition of the γS between the GDP- and GTP-bound states.
The crystal structures of the archaeal aIF2γ subunit in four different conformations (GTP-bound, GDP-formate, GDP, and nucleotide-free) have been determined.
the γ subunit from archaeal translation initiation factors (aIF2) undergoes large structural changes during the `life cycle' of aIF2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of the regulation of eIF2 by GTP hydrolysis, which is crucial to the control of protein synthesis.
the structure, dynamics and function of proteins.
the structural characterization of the γ subunit (eIF2γ) of the archaeal heterotrimeric initiation factor 2, aIF2γ, and the description of its conformational transitions in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the conformational changes in the aIF1γ subunit are driven by the nucleotide state and are not a result of the binding of the aIF2β subunit.
the aIF2 subunit undergoes a conformational transition from the GDP-bound to the GTP-bound form.

the crystal structures reported herein describe the different states in the aIF/2γ life cycle, and that these structures provide the first atomic details of aIF2 and the conformational changes that occur during its life cycle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the aIF-2γ-GTP state, the C-terminus is in an `out' conformation and the N-terminus is `in'.
the conformational changes in aIF2γ are driven by the binding and hydrolysis of GTP.
the aIF2 system is more complex than previously anticipated, and that aIF2 is a more versatile factor than the simple `GTPase' it was previously believed to be.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conformational changes in the eIF2γ switch are not as dramatic as previously thought, and that the conformation of the switch is more flexible than anticipated.
the GDP-formate structure is the most similar to the GTP-bound structure, and that this structure is the one that is most likely to be the `active state' of aIF2.
aIF2γ is a highly dynamic protein that undergoes significant conformational changes upon nucleotide binding and hydrolysis, as well as in the presence of P(i).
